quote: I'm hearing all this stuff that, you know, if you live in the ZIP code, it's free, and I don't know how true that is. Blah blah blah.
stewart_read: This is a too-good-to-be-true / scam-adjacent skepticism cue dropped early in the call — the customer is flagging that she's heard exaggerated marketing claims and isn't sure what to believe. The rep never directly addresses or corrects this misconception; he moves straight into verify questions.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may have judged that starting the qualifying questions immediately would build credibility faster than debating marketing claims — a legitimate sequencing choice given she was already cooperative.
coaching_implication: Flag for the rep: when a customer voices a specific skepticism ('is this actually free,' 'blah blah blah'), a one-line honest correction ('no, it's not free — it's a purchase or financing based on your usage') builds trust cheaper than letting it sit unaddressed until the closer call.

quote: I'm a widow now, and the bills are crazy when you live alone and you only have one income coming in.
stewart_read: Customer discloses widowhood and single-income financial strain unprompted — a trust gift per the schema. The rep's next line moves straight into the verify pitch without acknowledging it.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may have intentionally kept things brisk to avoid dwelling on a sensitive topic the customer raised casually rather than tearfully — but the transcript shows no acknowledgment at all, even a brief one.
coaching_implication: Coach a short acknowledgment reflex: 'I'm sorry to hear that, and I get why the bill on one income stings' before moving to questions. Costs two seconds, builds real rapport on a disclosure this specific.

quote: But come July, August, September, it's close to 800 because of sprinklers and dehumidifiers and air conditioning.
stewart_read: Customer volunteers a striking seasonal bill anchor ($250 winter / near $800 summer) unprompted. The rep's response is a flat 'Okay. Yeah. Yeah.' with no reflection or flip into emotional alignment against the utility.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may be deferring the emotional flip deliberately to the specialist call, treating his own role as pure data capture — but nothing in the transcript signals this was a conscious choice versus simply not registering the number.
coaching_implication: This is the clearest missed bill-anchor flip on the call. Coach: 'wow, $800 in the summer — that's exactly the kind of bill solar is built to take a bite out of' turns her own number into her reason to act, rather than filing it silently.

quote: Okay. I'm picking up dead sticks that had fallen from the winter, and I have and I was just yakking with my neighbor who, god bless him, burns the dead wood for me.
stewart_read: After the rep's flustered 'why can't I think right now' moment and the late 'how are you doing' catch-up, the customer volunteers an extended, good-humored story rather than pulling back — the self-deprecating apology at 03:37-03:48 successfully repaired the stumble.
coaching_implication: This is a positive example worth showing the rep directly: owning a mistake with humor ('you should've started with that one' / 'that can be your excuse') kept a talkative, warming customer engaged rather than embarrassed.

quote: No. I can't do that. I'm not that educated.
stewart_read: Customer explicitly signals she cannot handle a photo-text request unassisted. The schema's protocol calls for a pivot to verbal read-back within about 2 minutes of this kind of friction; instead the rep asks what phone she has and keeps working the photo/text path. Total elapsed time from bill-in-hand (03:14) to confirmed sent photo (08:04) runs close to five minutes.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep did eventually succeed in getting a usable photo, so the outcome was fine on this call — but the elapsed time shows the pivot decision point was missed, not that the persistence was wrong in principle.
coaching_implication: Coach on speed of pivot recognition: when a customer says 'I'm not that educated' about tech, the 2-minute budget should trigger an offer to just read the numbers off the bill as a fallback, rather than continuing to troubleshoot the phone/text path for several more minutes.

quote: if it's gonna be more than that, don't waste your time.
stewart_read: Customer states a hard cost ceiling ('at the most, like, $2 out of my pocket') and threatens to disqualify the appointment if it isn't met. The rep reassures generically ('We got great programs. You're gonna love what we have') rather than using her own $800 summer bill or her declared debt-free stance as leverage.
alternative_hypothesis: Reassurance without overpromising specific numbers is arguably the correct move at setter stage per numeric_discipline — the rep may be avoiding a promise he can't back with real figures.
coaching_implication: The rep was right not to quote numbers, but missed the chance to redirect: tying her own bill pain ('that's exactly why the specialist runs the numbers against what you're already paying') would have addressed the cost anxiety without fabricating figures.

quote: I don't want anything that I'm gonna have to owe over time. I'm debt free. I don't wanna owe anything.
stewart_read: Customer sets an explicit financial constraint on the appointment — debt-free status, no financing accepted — right before the appointment is booked. The rep doesn't address this specifically, moving straight to scheduling.
coaching_implication: This constraint must travel to the closer verbatim — booking around it without flagging it risks a wasted sit if the closer opens with financing options she's already ruled out.
